newsitem.title: israel: Israel cautions Arafat on Jewish settlers issue.
newsitem.headline: Israel cautions Arafat on Jewish settlers issue.

text.p: Israel warned Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat that he would set back peace moves if his negotiators pressed the issue of Jewish settlements at resumed talks on Sunday.

Foreign Minister David Levy, due to head Israel's team to the talks, was answering a warning from Arafat on Saturday that Israel would gamble with peace if it expanded settlements on occupied Arab land.
"I would propose to Arafat that he not repeat his declarations of this sort," Levy told Israel Radio. "The matter of settlements...certainly isn't on the agenda."
"If they want to delay the process, go ahead," Levy told army radio in another interview. "There is nothing in an atmosphere of declarations and threats to advance the process even a millimetre."
Levy and Mahmoud Abbas, the Palestinian chief negotiator also known as Abu Mazen, were due to convene eight joint committees to discuss expanding Palestinian rule.
About 130,000 Jews live in settlements scattered among the more than two million Palestinians of the West Bank and Gaza Strip captured by Israel in the 1967 Middle East war.

The settlements are one of several crucial "final-status" issues to be resolved in talks due to start up again next month. Palestinians fear Israel will speed up expansion of settlements, imposing facts on the ground in advance of future pullbacks.
Arafat called on Israel to respect a March 7 deadline for the first of three planned Israeli withdrawals from West Bank rural areas due to end by mid-1998.
"We hope that Israel will implement its promises," Arafat told reporters in self-ruled Jenin in the West Bank.

The stage for the talks was set when Arafat and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu met last week to follow up a U.S.-brokered breakthrough allowing the Palestinians to take over most of the West Bank town of Hebron.

The agenda, set by a U.S. annex to the Hebron deal, covers arrangements for Palestinian sea and air ports, a "safe passage" between the West Bank and Gaza, economic, civil and financial affairs and "people to people" cooperation.

Israeli Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai, on a tour of Hebron on Sunday, told reporters: "Every issue will be discussed accurately and in an orderly fashion, from the security perspective and other perspectives.

"In all there is an intention to make progress in the process itself and all subjects on the agenda," he said during a visit that included a walk in an Arab market and talks with settlers, both on the Israeli-held side of the volatile town.

Arafat, despite the momentum created by the Hebron handover and Israel's release of 30 Palestinian women prisoners last week, said: "The current Israeli government gambles with the peace process if settlement activity is increased".

Netanyahu, visiting the United States, faces growing dissent meanwhile from his own Likud party and right-wing coalition partners who say he must accelerate building projects for Jews in the West Bank and Arab East Jerusalem.
Mordechai told reporters: "New settlements will not be and have not been built".
